explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF explicitly leaves row-count messages enabled for every statement in usp_TestProcedure, adding DONE_IN_PROC traffic and confusing clients that consume result sets.
SET XACT_ABORT OFF while the procedure uses BEGIN TRANSACTION (lines 181, 238) allows statement-level errors to leave a partially applied, still-open transaction.
SELECT * FROM Sales.Orders returns all 16 columns including three nvarchar(MAX) columns, coupling callers to schema changes and wasting I/O and bandwidth.
SELECT TOP (10) o.OrderID from Sales.Orders has no ORDER BY, so the ten orders returned are arbitrary and can change between executions.
DISTINCT on o.OrderID is redundant because OrderID is the primary key of Sales.Orders; it forces a needless sort/hash aggregate.
WITH (NOLOCK) on Sales.Orders allows dirty reads, missing rows and duplicated rows from page splits.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) = 2016 wraps the date column in a function, preventing a range seek on OrderDate; use OrderDate >= '20160101' AND OrderDate < '20170101'.
o.CustomerID (int) is compared to @CustomerIdText (nvarchar(20)); the int side is implicitly converted, degrading cardinality estimates and seek behaviour on FK_Sales_Orders_CustomerID.
@CustomerID IS NULL OR o.CustomerID = @CustomerID is catch-all filtering that produces a single cached plan with poor estimates and a scan of Sales.Orders.
o.Comments LIKE N'%urgent%' starts with a wildcard, so no index can seek; the nvarchar(MAX) Comments column must be fully scanned.
o.CustomerID NOT IN (SELECT i.CustomerID FROM Sales.Invoices) returns no rows at all if any CustomerID in the subquery is NULL; use NOT EXISTS.
ISNULL(o.CustomerID, 0) = 1 wraps the indexed CustomerID column, blocking an index seek on FK_Sales_Orders_CustomerID.
o.OrderID + 0 = @OrderID applies arithmetic to the primary key column, forcing a scan of Sales.Orders instead of a clustered index seek.
o.CustomerID <> 1 is an inequality that matches nearly every row, so the index on CustomerID cannot be seeked meaningfully.
CROSS JOIN of Sales.Orders and Sales.Customers has no join predicate, producing a full product of both tables before TOP (1) discards rows.
Sales.Orders AS o, Sales.OrderLines AS ol uses comma-join syntax with the join condition in WHERE; use an explicit INNER JOIN ON o.OrderID = ol.OrderID.
The correlated COUNT(*) against Sales.OrderLines is evaluated once per Sales.Orders row; a grouped derived table or OUTER APPLY would compute it set-wise.
EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE ol.OrderID = o.OrderID AND ol.Quantity > 1) is a per-row correlated probe that can be expressed as a join to a filtered, grouped set.
CASE WHEN o.Comments IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END is duplicated in the select list and ORDER BY, so it is evaluated twice and must be maintained in two places.
ORDER BY 2 sorts by select-list position; adding or reordering columns silently changes the sort to a different column.
OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY ordered only by o.OrderDate, which is not unique in Sales.Orders; pages can repeat or skip orders. Add OrderID as a tie-breaker.
The two branches filter OrderID = 1 and OrderID = 2 on a primary key, so they are disjoint; UNION adds a pointless distinct sort.
(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Sales.OrderLines ...) > 0 counts every matching order line when EXISTS would stop at the first row.
SELECT @OrderID = o.OrderID FROM Sales.Orders assigns from an unordered multi-row set, silently keeping an arbitrary last value; use SET with a scalar subquery or TOP (1) with ORDER BY.
@OrderIds is a table variable fed from Sales.Orders; on older compatibility levels it is estimated as one row and has no column statistics, producing bad downstream plans.
INSERT @OrderIds ... SELECT TOP (5) o.OrderID has no ORDER BY, so which five orders are stored is arbitrary.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders creates the temp table schema implicitly, taking schema-modification locks in tempdb and hiding column types/indexes.
SELECT TOP (5) o.OrderID INTO #ImplicitOrders lacks ORDER BY, so the persisted five rows are nondeterministic.
order_cursor iterates Sales.Orders one OrderID at a time (OPEN/FETCH NEXT at lines 97-98) for work that a single set-based statement can do.
WHILE @Counter <= 1 performs iterative single-row work with SET @Counter += 1 instead of a set-based operation.
@Sql is built by concatenating CONVERT(nvarchar(20), @CustomerID) into the statement text, generating a distinct plan per value and an injection-prone pattern.
EXEC (@Sql) executes a concatenated string with no parameter binding, so values are not typed and plans are not reused.
@Sql concatenates CONVERT(nvarchar(20), @OrderID) into the WHERE clause text instead of leaving a @OrderID placeholder in the statement.
sys.sp_executesql is called with only @Sql and no parameter definition list, so the embedded OrderID value is not parameterized.
#Scratch is created but never dropped, keeping tempdb objects and metadata alive until the procedure scope ends.
The CATCH block only runs SELECT ERROR_MESSAGE() AS IgnoredError; the failure (e.g. divide-by-zero at line 121) is hidden from the caller with no THROW or failure return code.
RAISERROR (N'Negative order ID', 16, 1) uses the legacy error API; THROW preserves the original error and honours XACT_ABORT.
PRINT N'Monster procedure diagnostic' emits buffered, unstructured text that clients may not receive until the batch flushes.
o.CustomerID = 1 hard-codes a business identifier instead of using the @CustomerID parameter.
o.OrderDate >= '20160101' embeds an unlabelled date constant in the query; it should be a named parameter or documented variable.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') has no style argument, so the result depends on the session DATEFORMAT/language and can mean Jan 2 or Feb 1.
COALESCE(o.CustomerID, 0) = COALESCE(i.CustomerID, 0) wraps both join columns, preventing index seeks and hash/merge join optimization on CustomerID.
Sales.Orders is joined to itself on OrderID = OrderID only to return o.OrderID, which is already available from the single row; the join adds a redundant access.
ORDER BY o.Comments sorts on an nvarchar(MAX) column, causing a huge, unselective sort with likely tempdb spills.
SUM(ol.Quantity) scans the entire fact-like Sales.OrderLines table with no WHERE restriction.
HAVING ol.OrderID > 0 is a row-level predicate on a grouping column; moving it to WHERE filters rows before aggregation.
COUNT(*) without GROUP BY returns exactly one row, so ORDER BY OrderCount does nothing.
MERGE into Sales.Orders has documented concurrency/upsert race and constraint edge cases; use separate IF EXISTS / UPDATE / INSERT logic.
UPDATE Sales.Orders SET Comments = Comments writes the existing value back, incurring locking, logging and trigger/version-store work for no data change.
DELETE FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE Quantity = -1 deletes on a non-key business value, potentially removing an unbounded number of order lines.
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01' blocks a worker thread inside the procedure instead of using asynchronous scheduling.
BEGIN TRANSACTION at line 181 is outside any TRY/CATCH, so an error before the ROLLBACK at line 182 can leave an orphaned open transaction holding locks.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT Sales.Orders ON changes session-scoped state and couples the procedure to manual identity management on a shared table.
EXEC sp_who is not schema-qualified (and uses the sp_ prefix), forcing extra name resolution in master and risking a wrong procedure being executed.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 is never reset to 0, so every subsequent SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE in this session (including the writes below) is silently limited to one row.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories VALUES (99, @NewCategory) omits the column list, so the insert breaks or mis-maps values if the temp table's column order changes.
CategoryID 99 is a magic business identifier embedded in the VALUES clause instead of being supplied as a parameter or looked up.
CustomerName LIKE '%' + @CustomerName + '%' begins with a wildcard, so UQ_Sales_Customers_CustomerName cannot be seeked and Sales.Customers is scanned.
@CustomerName is concatenated straight into the LIKE literal of @sql; a value containing a quote can break out and execute arbitrary SQL.
sp_executesql is executed with only the concatenated @sql string and no parameter definitions, so @CustomerName is never bound as a parameter.
sp_executesql is called without the sys schema qualifier, relying on implicit system-procedure resolution.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers SET CustomerCategoryID = 1 has no WHERE clause and rewrites every row loaded into the temp table.
CustomerCategoryID is set to the magic value 1 rather than a parameter or a looked-up category key.
WHERE o.OrderDate >= '2016-01-01' filters the LEFT JOINed Sales.Orders side, eliminating NULL-extended rows and silently turning the outer join into an inner join.
The unlabelled constant '2016-01-01' is embedded in the OrderDate filter instead of being passed as a dated parameter.
WHERE DeliveryMethodID = NULL never evaluates to true under ANSI nulls, so the query always returns zero rows; use IS NULL.
dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) in the select list is evaluated per row of Sales.Customers and blocks parallelism (unless the UDF is inlined).
This CATCH block only runs SELECT ERROR_MESSAGE(); the DELETE/COMMIT failure is never rethrown and no failure status is returned to the caller.
The transaction opened at line 238 is not rolled back in this CATCH block, leaving an uncommittable/open transaction that holds locks after the procedure exits.
WITH (INDEX = 1) hard-codes an index ID on Sales.Customers, freezing the plan and breaking if index 1 is dropped or renumbered.
The FROM clause introduces three levels of nested derived tables (t1/t2/t3) that each only project CustomerID; flatten into a single query or CTE.
CustomerName LIKE '%A%' inside the innermost derived table starts with a wildcard, forcing a full scan of Sales.Customers.
SELECT * FROM dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti(@CustomerName) depends on the function's current column set and returns columns callers may not need.
dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti is a multi-statement TVF, which is optimized as a black box with a fixed row estimate; an inline TVF would be expanded into the outer query.
